articles.title: Why a Fixed Choreography Is the Secret to Reliable Two-Subject AI Video
articles.description: There is a quiet argument happening inside every text-to-video demo. One side says: give the model the most freedom you can, and it will surprise you. The other side says: freedom is where the artifacts live. The scream-and-swap dance trend — two photos in, one 21-second vertical clip out — has already picked a side, and I think it picked correctly. It gives the model almost nothing to improvise. That is not a shortcut. It is the entire reason the output works. Free-form generation is a reliability tax When you ask a video diffusion model for "two people dancing together," you are implicitly asking it to solve several hard problems at once: consistent identity for two distinct subjects, plausible motion that respects a beat, spatial layout that keeps two bodies from merging, and temporal coherence across every frame. Each of those problems compounds the others. A model that gets four out of four right on a lucky seed is a model you still cannot ship a product on, because the fifth generation is the one your user sees. Consumer video tools learned this the hard way. The products that stuck are not the ones with the most expressive prompt box. They are the ones that shrank the problem until a modest model could clear it every time. The scream-and-swap format is constraint engineering Look at what the format actually fixes in place: A hard 21-second duration. No variable length, no pacing decisions for the model to make. Two fixed slots. Photo A takes the close-up scream first while Photo B dances behind; then they swap; then both run forward together. The role order is a parameter you pick, not something the model invents. A fixed camera grammar. Vertical 720p, a single framing language, a locked musical cue. The model is not asked to direct — only to render. No prompt. The instruction is the structure itself. You feed two faces and a slot assignment; the choreography is already decided. Every one of those constraints removes a dimension where diffusion models fail unpredictably. Identity drift, subject-swap, limb merging, tempo mismatch — these are all failure modes that a free-form prompt invites and a fixed choreography excludes. The developers are not dumbing the product down. They are engineering the model's way into its own competence band, where Seedance 2.5 (the generation backend) can produce consistent two-subject results at consumer prices instead of studio prices. Why "no prompt" is a reliability feature, not a UX gap The most misunderstood part of this format is the missing text box. "You just upload two photos and it works" sounds, to a developer, like a product that did not bother to expose its controls. The opposite is true. The absence of a prompt is the loudest signal of intent: the team moved the entire burden of choreography out of the model's responsibility and into a fixed template, because free-form choreography was the thing that broke consistency. This is a genuinely transferable idea. If you are building any generative product where a user expects a predictable result rather than an inspired one, ask yourself which of your model's inputs are really free variables and which should be constants. The scream-and-swap format is a masterclass in shrinking the free-variable set to the smallest thing that still feels expressive — two faces and a role order — and letting everything else be a constant. What the user still owns Two things survive all that constraint, and they are the two things that matter emotionally: whose faces and which one goes first. That is the entire creative surface, and it is enough. The fact that a fixed format still feels like yours is proof that expressiveness does not scale with degrees of freedom. There is one dimension the template cannot and should not automate: consent. Before you feed anyone else's face into a generator — a friend, a partner, a coworker, a stranger's photo — you need their permission. That is not a technical guardrail; it is a precondition. A fixed choreography makes the video reliable. It does not make the people in it yours to use. This is the one variable that stays firmly on the human side, and it is worth saying in every article on the topic because it is the one part no constraint can ever get right for you. The takeaway for builders If you are evaluating a two-subject video tool — or building one — the useful question is not "how expressive is the prompt." It is "how much of the problem has already been solved by the template, and what is left for the model to get wrong." A product that answers that question honestly is one you can build trust on. The scream-and-swap trend — including the tool that runs it at smalltownboyai.app — is a working reference implementation of that principle: constrain the choreography, keep the two faces and the swap order as the only free variables, and let a mid-sized model clear a hard problem reliably at a $9.90 price point instead of a render-farm price point. That is not less AI. That is better AI, pointed at the part of the problem it can actually solve.

articles.title: John Carmack deleted fast_inverse_sqrt() in 1999. In commit c51b980a, he replaced 0x5f3759df. We held an air-gapped séance with its ghost.
articles.description: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine John Carmack deleted fast_inverse_sqrt() in 1999. In commit c51b980a of the Quake III source tree, he replaced the infamous magic constant 0x5f3759df with a hardware SSE rsqrtss instruction. Sixteen lines of legendary, dark-arts floating-point bit hacking—accompanied by the immortal comment // what the fuck?—were struck down in a single routine commit. Every git repository on earth is a cemetery like this. Functions that fought off brutal midnight outages are refactored away. Classes sculpted over cold winter weekends are vaporized with a callous four-word commit message: "refactor: remove legacy worker". And the worst part? We don't even remember their names. When you look back at an old codebase, you remember what the function felt like, or the bug it cured. You never remember the commit hash. For the finale of Hacktoberfest 2026—bringing us Halloween on October 31 and Día de los Muertos on November 1–2—we built NecroGit: an air-gapped terminal séance and candlelit digital ofrenda for deleted code, powered by local Google Gemma 2 and pure Python Standard Library. 🎨 The Whole Project in One Picture (Xiaohei Edition) Xiaohei exhuming a departed def legacy_worker() scroll from the .git/objects crypt with mechanical tongs onto the candlelit marigold ofrenda altar powered by local Google Gemma 2, completely air-gapped from cloud AI. 🕯️ What I Built NecroGit is a zero-dependency, local-first code necromancy engine with two presentation surfaces: The Amber Phosphor CRT Terminal (--scan & --seance): A high-speed POSIX CLI and retro terminal interface that parses .git object trees, unearthing dead functions, deprecated classes, and whole deleted files. The Digital Remembrance Ofrenda: A browser altar featuring 45 floating cempasúchil (marigold) petals rendered on HTML5 canvas, animated candle flames, and a zero-API procedural Web Audio synthesizer that generates authentic 60 Hz CRT flyback hum, pink noise cemetery wind drafts, mechanical key clicks, and singing bowl chimes. The Sovereign Gemma 2 Séance Engine: Uses Google's open-weight Gemma 2 (via local Ollama) to inhabit the spirit of the deceased code. articles.title: How to Break Through MRR Stagnation and Scale Again
articles.description: For months, maybe even years, your SaaS dashboard has looked the same. New users are coming in, marketing is running, and your product is active, but your Monthly Recurring Revenue (MRR) is not growing. It feels like you are working harder, yet the results remain unchanged. This situation is called MRR stagnation, and it is one of the most dangerous phases for any SaaS business. It looks stable on the surface, but internally, growth has already slowed or stopped. In this guide, we will understand why SaaS companies hit this growth ceiling and how to break through it using practical, proven strategies. What is MRR Stagnation? MRR stagnation happens when your revenue stops increasing month over month, even though customer activity continues. It occurs when new revenue is completely balanced out by lost revenue from churn or downgrades. As a result, total MRR stays flat. In simple terms, your business is running but not moving forward. When Net New MRR = 0, your business is stagnant. This means growth does not only depend on acquiring customers, but it also depends on improving retention, pricing, and expansion revenue. The “Leaky Bucket” Problem in SaaS If your MRR is flat, the first thing to understand is the leaky bucket problem. You are pouring water (new customers) into a bucket, but there are holes at the bottom (churn and downgrades). No matter how much water you add, the level never rises. To fix stagnation, you must first plug these leaks before focusing on scaling acquisition. Fixing Customer Churn First Churn is the biggest reason behind MRR stagnation. If customers leave quickly, your revenue will never grow consistently. Churn can be divided into two types: Voluntary churn: Customers actively cancel because they don’t find value Involuntary churn: Payment failures, expired cards, or billing issues In many SaaS businesses, involuntary churn alone can account for a significant revenue loss. Reducing Churn with Better Systems To reduce churn, you need strong retention systems: Improve onboarding experience so users reach value faster Use lifecycle emails and in-app guidance Fix failed payments using dunning management tools Conduct exit surveys to understand cancellation reasons When churn reduces, MRR automatically stabilises, and growth becomes easier. Achieving Negative Churn (The SaaS Growth Engine) The ultimate goal for SaaS businesses is negative churn. This happens when revenue gained from existing customers (upsells, upgrades, add-ons) is higher than revenue lost from cancellations. In this stage, even without new customers, your revenue grows every month. This is why expansion revenue is more powerful than acquisition alone. Why Your Pricing Strategy Might Be Blocking Growth Many SaaS companies fail to revisit their pricing for years. This creates hidden revenue limitations. If your pricing is too simple or outdated, it can directly lead to stagnation. Moving to Value-Based Pricing Instead of charging per user or fixed plans, consider pricing based on value delivered: Usage-based pricing (storage, API calls, transactions) Tiered plans with clear upgrade paths Paid add-ons like premium support or advanced analytics This creates natural opportunities for revenue expansion. The Product-Led Growth Trap Many SaaS companies grow quickly using product-led growth (PLG) in the early stages. However, after a point, growth slows down because the initial market gets saturated. This is when companies hit the PLG ceiling. Moving Upmarket to Break Stagnation To break this ceiling, many SaaS companies move upmarket: Target enterprise customers instead of SMBs Introduce annual contracts instead of monthly billing Build advanced security features like SOC2 compliance Create dedicated sales and account management teams Although the acquisition becomes slower, revenue per customer increases significantly. Fixing Your SaaS Marketing Funnel If retention is strong but MRR is still flat, the problem often lies in acquisition quality. Not all traffic is valuable traffic. Focus on High-Intent SEO and BOFU Content Instead of general awareness blogs, focus on high-conversion content like: Competitor comparison pages Case studies with real ROI results Industry-specific landing pages This improves conversion rates and brings in higher-value customers. Improve LTV to CAC Ratio A healthy SaaS business should maintain: LTV : CAC ≥ 3 : 1 If your acquisition cost is too high compared to customer lifetime value, your growth will always remain limited. Expansion Revenue: The Real Growth Multiplier Expansion revenue is the most powerful lever for breaking MRR stagnation. It allows you to grow revenue from existing customers instead of constantly relying on new ones. Key Expansion Strategies Upselling: Upgrade users from Basic to Pro plans Cross-selling: Offer complementary tools or services Add-ons: Sell extra features or increased limits These strategies significantly improve Net Revenue Retention (NRR) and create predictable growth. Understanding Your SaaS Growth Ceiling Every SaaS business has a theoretical growth ceiling based on churn and acquisition efficiency. If churn is high and expansion revenue is low, your ceiling will be very limited. But if retention is strong and expansion is growing, your ceiling keeps increasing over time. This is why mature SaaS companies focus more on retention and expansion than just new customer acquisition. Conclution MRR stagnation is not the end of growth; it is a signal that your business model needs optimisation. Instead of pushing harder on acquisition alone, you need to balance three core pillars: Reduce churn Increase expansion revenue Improve pricing and positioning When these three elements work together, your SaaS business moves beyond the growth ceiling and enters a scalable, compounding growth phase.

articles.title: crustc ports rustc to C and builds it with GCC
articles.description: The crustc repository is C code that you compile with GCC and GNU make into a working Rust compiler. Point make at a matching LLVM build and the binary it produces reports rustc 1.98.0-nightly (c712ea946 2026-06-16), then goes on to build core, alloc and std. The author built it on ARM64 Linux with GCC 13.3.0 and the LLD 18.1.3 linker. An unoptimized build takes about 78 seconds of wall time (937 seconds of user time with make -j20). It still needs LLVM at runtime, because rustc uses LLVM, so the repo asks you to supply libLLVM.so.22.1-rust-1.98.0-nightly from the matching nightly toolchain rather than shipping a binary. That is rustc itself, translated to C and built by a C compiler. The repo is a demo for cilly, the author's Rust-to-C toolchain and, by their count, the 14th attempt at the problem over three years (rustc_codegen_clr was an earlier public one). cilly is a Rust library that generates C plus a rustc backend plugin. Instead of handing MIR to LLVM for machine code, it emits C and passes that to whatever C compiler you nominate for the target. Compiling rustc with itself through that path is the flashiest thing to show, so that is what the repo does. The useful engineering is that cilly does not assume a fixed C dialect. It emits "witness" programs and compiles them to learn what the target compiler and platform actually support: a file containing _Thread_local int KEYWORD_TLS_SUPPORTED; only compiles if the compiler has _Thread_local, so that tells cilly whether it can use the keyword. It queries type layouts, sizes, alignments, character encoding (ASCII) and integer representation (two's complement), with fallbacks where it can. The author aims to assume nothing outside ANSI C, works around newer-standard hazards like strict aliasing, and documents the few unavoidable assumptions ((void*)(uintptr_t)(ptr) round-trips, CHAR_BIT == 8) with runtime asserts where possible. The cost is that output is target-specific. C generated for Arm64 will not run on riscv32; you regenerate per target. cilly can also talk to a C compiler over TCP, with UART floated as a possibility. You run rustc on an ordinary Linux box and let cilly drive a small C server on the target, which covers platforms that have no C cross-compiler at all. The author used this to build small Rust programs for x86 Plan 9 VMs from an Arm64 Linux host; the binary printed Hello, world! and carried a rust_begin_unwind symbol. cilly can embed markers in its object files, cache its IR, and emit a directory of makefiles, so the end product is a tree you build with a C compiler and make. Compiling Rust through C does not undo Rust's safety guarantees. The borrow checker and type system run in rustc's frontend, which cilly does not touch; crustc is rustc, so those checks still happen before any C is emitted. The change is in the codegen trust base: you are now relying on cilly's translation and a C compiler to be correct, on top of the documented assumptions above. The author is candid that the demo is rough. They are chasing optimization-related bugs and recommend building without optimizations, both because enabling them "may break stuff" and because they choke on larger Rust files. Generated code is mostly ABI-compatible with normal rustc output, with a known exception on Arm64, where rustc picks an sret convention that C cannot express for small structs under 16 bytes. The target user is anyone who maintains Rust that people keep asking to run on old or obscure hardware, the recurring "Rust doesn't support Plan 9" objection whenever a project moves off C. The stated goal is targets that have a C compiler but no LLVM or GCC Rust backend. It is not there yet. The author says cilly is not ready for public consumption and that real use waits on the full toolchain. crustc is the evidence it works: a Rust compiler that builds from C with stock GCC and make, self-hosting included.
